Triggers.value: Difficulty breathing or feeling short of breath

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Being around people in authority or uniform

Threat.value: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger

Memory.value: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again
I have to be on guard all the time
The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down

issues.item: Triggers: Being Followed: Feeling followed or tracked
issues.explanation: For toxic chemical exposure, 'being followed or tracked' suggests an interpersonal/persecutory trauma context that is not supported by the other selected items and is hard to reconcile with the trauma type.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
issues.explanation: The threat profile is dominated by interpersonal assault-style vigilance to sounds and sudden movements, which does not fit well with the stated trauma of toxic chemical exposure unless there is additional unreported violent context.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
issues.explanation: 'People are not what they seem' implies mistrust of others in a deceptive or persecutory sense; paired with 'being followed' it shifts the formulation toward interpersonal threat rather than contamination/exposure-related PTSD.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Distrust Others: People are not what they seem
issues.explanation: 'Avoid authority figures' is difficult to connect to the rest of the profile and to toxic chemical exposure specifically; no other items indicate authority-linked fear, blame, or trauma reminders involving uniforms/institutions.

vignette: The ruptured canister in the abandoned dye factory still played in Elena's mind not as a closed case file, but as a suffocating present. She had been tracing illegal waste dumps when a pressurized drum split, spitting a thick, acrid vapor that clung to the damp concrete. When she finally dragged herself toward the loading bay, her lungs burned and refused to draw full breaths. The hazmat team arrived in stiff protective gear, scrubbing her arms with aggressive antiseptic wipes that stung her skin and flooded the narrow alley with a sharp, clinical stench. She remembered pressing her palms over her face to shield it from their unyielding uniforms, then mentally forcing herself to count structural steel beams to stop the panic from swallowing her. She never quite managed to piece together which valve had failed or how the ventilation system gave way; her recollections arrived as disjointed snapshots, and she quickly learned to push those gaps away before they solidified. The hospital smell and the phantom scent of the rescue team's sweat would later ignite the same choking sensation, and because the memories felt so vivid, so undeniably alive in the room with her, she convinced herself the danger had not passed. That lingering terror convinced her that the agency had abandoned her during the spill, cementing a quiet, permanent belief that she would never again feel safe or experience normal affection. In the months that followed, Elena's detective work grew increasingly difficult. When a shift commander called her into the precinct's evidence bay for a routine safety debrief, she immediately turned her chair toward the wall and found herself reciting case file numbers aloud until the meeting ended. Her body never truly relaxed on the job. She found herself scanning the perimeter of every crime scene, bracing at the sudden crack of a car backfiring or the sharp bark of a patrol radio, her muscles coiled tight as if anticipating another release of invisible poison. She had come to believe she must remain on perpetual guard, which meant scanning every doorway and flinching at every echo. That conviction also seeped into her perception of the air itself; a whiff of another officer's gym sweat near the locker rooms or the faint scent of antiseptic from a clinic waiting room would instantly spike her pulse, convincing her that the same suffocating cloud was returning. She had come to believe the people who should have protected her had let her down, and because she was always scanning, always braced for the next sound, her body remained wired for escape, which meant the sensory triggers would only grow more potent, feeding the very fear they provoked. Now, at fifty-seven, Elena sat in her dimly lit living room, the weight of years pressing on her shoulders. The habits she had cultivated were no longer choices but reflexes. When the neighbor's garbage truck coughed a diesel puff that carried the faint tang of industrial cleaner, her breath hitched and her shoulders locked. The sensory spike immediately flooded her mind with fragmented images of the factory floor, and because the memories felt present rather than past, she convinced herself the threat was ongoing. Her instinct was to cross her arms over her face and mentally force herself to think of her old patrol routes, but the very act of shutting down only convinced her that her mind was failing, that she was permanently broken. That belief tightened her posture further, convincing her she must remain on perpetual guard, which meant scanning every sound and bracing at every echo. And because she was always scanning, her body stayed on alert, which meant a single whiff of a coworker's sweat or the sterile smell of a clinic waiting room would instantly resurrect the terror, feeding the conviction that the institution had left her to suffocate alone. She finally made the appointment after a patrol sergeant asked her to testify at a departmental review. The thought of standing in front of microphones and uniformed officials made her palms sweat and her chest constrict until she couldn't speak. She was terrified of collapsing on the stand, but beneath that fear was a quiet, desperate hope that someone might finally help her unclench the vise she had been wearing for years, even if she suspected the feeling of calm might never truly return.
